Histiocytic syndromes cover a broad range of proliferative disorders of histiocytes (mac- rophages and dendritic cells), for which the classification and diagnostic criteria are evolving.1 Langerhans-cell his- tiocytosis (histiocytosis X) is one such disorder character- ised by proliferation of CD1 positive Langerhans cells (a form of dendritic cell).1 Terms that were formerly used for different clinical manifestations of Langerhans-cell histio- cytosis include eosinophilic granuloma, Hand-Schüller- Christian disease, and Letterer-Siwe syndrome,1-4 but these are now considered obsolete.1 Langerhans-cell histi- ocytosis mainly presents in childhood, and is of uncertain aetiology: it is not clear whether it should be considered a malignancy.4,5 The clinical presentation of Langerhans-cell histiocytosis is highly variable.2,3,6,7 The classic feature is single or mul- tiple bone lesions, and skin lesions may also occur (single system, localised, or restricted disease).3-5,7 The disorder may also involve lymph nodes or visceral organs, ulti- mately causing dysfunction of the liver, lungs, or bone marrow (extensive or multisystem disease).4,5 Sequelae to the disease include diabetes insipidus, growth failure, and Antineoplastics 651 The symbol † denotes a preparation no longer actively marketed The symbol  denotes a substance whose use may be restricted in certain sports (see p.vii) orthopaedic handicap.3,6 The morbidity and prognosis de- pends upon the number of organ systems involved, and whether normal function of these organs is affected. Pa- tients with restricted disease have a generally benign course, and single lesions often regress spontaneously. However, if a bone lesion does not resolve, or risks causing fracture or deformity before it resolves, or is causing disa- bling symptoms, it may be treated with curettage, intrale- sional corticosteroids, or radiotherapy.
